reading.rtitle: Going to London on Business? Read the Fine Print First
paras: If you are a Brazilian lawyer and you are flying to London for meetings next month, there is one thing you are going to need before you even think about your itinerary: a travel authorization. Since 2025, most visitors who do not need a visa, Brazilians included, have had to apply online for an Electronic Travel Authorisation, known as an ETA, before they travel. It costs a small fee, most applications are decided within three working days, and once it is approved, it will be valid for two years, or until your passport expires, whichever comes first.

The authorization is not a visa, and it does not guarantee anything. When you land, a border officer will still decide whether to let you in. Most of the time, the conversation will last less than a minute. The officer will want to know why you are visiting, how long you are staying and where. Answer simply and precisely: I'm attending meetings with a client in the City, and I'm flying back on Friday. Travelers who give vague answers, or whose story changes halfway through, are the ones who get taken aside, and some of them are denied entry.

The real trap is in the fine print. As a business visitor, you can attend meetings, go to conferences, and negotiate and sign contracts. What you cannot do is work for a UK company, paid or unpaid. Many professionals do not see the line until they are standing on it. Attending a meeting with a client in London is a permitted activity. Spending three weeks inside that client's London office, doing the work their own team would normally do, is not. If your client is going to ask you to stay longer and help their team, that is a different visit, and it needs a different permission.

So before the trip, plan like a lawyer. Ask the company you are visiting for a letter of invitation that describes the meetings, not the work. Keep your return ticket and proof of funds in your bag, even if nobody asks for them. And check the dates: a visitor can usually stay for up to six months, but a business trip that was supposed to last a week and turns into three months will raise questions at the next border. By the time you board the plane, you will have done the boring part, and the only thing left to deal with will be the jet lag.

listenings.text: I advise people who travel to the UK for work, and the question I hear most often is: what am I going to say at the border? My answer is always the same: say less. The officer is going to ask you three things. Why are you here, how long are you staying, and where are you staying. If you are attending a conference, say that, and say when it ends. Do not explain the whole project. Do not mention that the client might offer you a job. The second thing I tell people is to read the fine print of their own plans. Last month a client of mine was flying in for two days of meetings, and then he told me that he was also going to spend a week training the London team. That is work, not a meeting, and it is not a permitted activity for a visitor. So we changed the plan. He will do the training online, from Sao Paulo, next month.

My trip to London is finally confirmed. I'm flying out of Sao Paulo on Sunday night, with a layover in Lisbon, and I land at Heathrow on Monday afternoon. The client is sending a car, so I'm not going to deal with the train and three suitcases. On Tuesday and Wednesday I'm meeting their legal team to negotiate the distribution agreement. If everything goes well, by Thursday evening we will have agreed on every clause except the price, and the price will be the partners' problem, not mine. I applied for my travel authorization six weeks ago, and it came back in two days. I'll be honest: the thing I am most worried about is not the border. It's the jet lag. I always think I will sleep on the plane, and I never do.

extra_audio.text: First, Pedro checks that his passport will still be valid for the whole trip. Then he applies online for the travel authorization, and it is approved two days later. Next, he asks the client in London for a letter of invitation that describes the meetings. A week before the flight, he prints his itinerary, his return ticket and his proof of funds. Finally, at Heathrow, he tells the border officer that he is attending meetings and flying back on Friday.
